name: ict_set2_p1
label: ICT: set 2 (software, operating systems, programming languages, computer operations, files, word processing, spreadsheets, databases, presentations and graphics)

papers.title: Types of Software: practice set 1
papers.description: 6 original WASSCE-style objective questions on types of software, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Which of the following is system software?
questions.explanation:
System software runs and manages the computer. The operating system is the main system software; utility programs, translators and device drivers are the others.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a word processor: A word processor does a task for the user, so it is application software.
- a spreadsheet program: A spreadsheet is an application package for calculations.
- a web browser: A browser is an application used to view web pages.

questions.stem: Antivirus programs are examples of
questions.explanation:
Utility programs maintain, protect or improve the computer. Antivirus, backup, disk cleanup, defragmenter and file compression programs are utilities, a kind of system software.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- application packages: Antivirus programs look after the computer itself, not a user task such as typing.
- device drivers: A device driver lets the operating system work with one hardware device.
- programming languages: A programming language is used to write programs.

questions.stem: Software written specially for one organisation to meet its exact needs is called
questions.explanation:
Bespoke (custom-written or tailor-made) software is written to order for one person or organisation. It fits their needs exactly but costs more and takes time to write.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- off-the-shelf software: Off-the-shelf software is ready-made and sold to many buyers.
- freeware: Freeware is software that is free to use.
- shareware: Shareware is free to try for a time, then must be paid for.

questions.stem: A small program that allows the operating system to communicate with a printer is called
questions.explanation:
Each hardware device, such as a printer, scanner or graphics card, needs its device driver so that the operating system can send it instructions.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a compiler: A compiler translates a high-level program into machine code.
- an antivirus program: An antivirus program finds and removes malware.
- a spreadsheet: A spreadsheet is an application for calculations.

questions.stem: Software whose source code can be freely read, changed and shared is called
questions.explanation:
Open-source software, such as Linux, LibreOffice and Firefox, makes its source code available for anyone to read, change and share, usually at no cost.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- shareware: Shareware may be tried free for a time; its code is not shared.
- proprietary software: Proprietary software is bought, and users may not copy or change it.
- bespoke software: Bespoke software is written for one organisation.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an advantage of off-the-shelf software over bespoke software?
questions.explanation:
Off-the-shelf software is cheaper because many buyers share the cost, is available immediately, and has been tested by many users; but it may not fit every need.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- It fits the organisation's needs exactly.  
  That is an advantage of bespoke software.
- It can be changed whenever the organisation wishes.  
  Bespoke software, not a ready-made package, can be changed to order.
- It is written for only one user.  
  Off-the-shelf software is written for many users.

options.label: A
options.content: It fits the organisation's needs exactly.

options.label: B
options.content: It can be changed whenever the organisation wishes.

options.label: C
options.content: It is written for only one user.

options.label: D
options.content: It is cheaper and available at once.

papers.title: Operating Systems: practice set 1
papers.description: 6 original WASSCE-style objective questions on operating systems, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a function of an operating system?
questions.explanation:
The operating system manages the processor, memory, files and devices, provides the user interface and security. Typing and formatting a letter is done by an application, a word processor.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- managing memory: Memory management is a main function of the operating system.
- managing files and folders: File management is a main function of the operating system.
- controlling input and output devices: Device management is a main function of the operating system.

questions.stem: An operating system that responds to input immediately, as needed to control traffic lights or an aircraft, is
questions.explanation:
A real-time operating system must react to events within a fixed, very short time, so it is used where delays would be dangerous: aircraft, medical machines, traffic control and factory robots.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a batch operating system: A batch system runs groups of jobs later, with no immediate response.
- a single-user, single-task operating system: This describes an old system such as MS-DOS, not its speed of response.
- a network operating system: A network operating system manages users, files and printers on a network.

questions.stem: In a graphical user interface, WIMP stands for
questions.explanation:
WIMP names the main parts of a graphical user interface: windows, icons, menus and a pointer controlled by a mouse or touchpad.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- windows, Internet, mouse, printer: The Internet and the printer are not parts of a GUI.
- words, images, menus, programs: W stands for windows and I for icons.
- windows, icons, monitors, processors: M stands for menus and P for the pointer.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a mobile operating system?
questions.explanation:
Android (by Google) and iOS (by Apple) are mobile operating systems, made for touch screens, battery life and wireless networks.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Microsoft Word: Microsoft Word is a word processor, an application.
- CorelDRAW: CorelDRAW is a graphics application.
- MS-DOS: MS-DOS was an early operating system for desktop PCs.

questions.stem: One advantage of a graphical user interface over a command-line interface is that it
questions.explanation:
In a GUI, users click or touch icons and menus they can see, so there is nothing to memorise; a CLI is faster for experts and uses fewer resources, but commands must be typed exactly.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- uses less memory and processing power: A command-line interface uses less memory.
- requires commands to be remembered and typed: Typed commands are a feature of a command-line interface.
- needs no pointing device: A GUI is normally used with a pointing device.

options.label: A
options.content: is easier for beginners to learn and use

options.label: B
options.content: uses less memory and processing power

options.label: C
options.content: requires commands to be remembered and typed

questions.stem: The ability of an operating system to run two or more programs at the same time is called
questions.explanation:
Multitasking lets you, for example, play music while typing a document; the operating system shares the processor's time between the programs.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- booting: Booting is starting the computer.
- formatting: Formatting prepares a disk, or changes the look of a document.
- compiling: Compiling translates a program into machine code.

papers.title: Programming Languages and Translators: practice set 1
papers.description: 7 original WASSCE-style objective questions on programming languages and translators, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: The only language that a computer's processor understands directly is
questions.explanation:
Machine language is made of binary codes (0s and 1s) that the CPU carries out directly. Every other language must be translated into it.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- assembly language: Assembly language must first be translated by an assembler.
- a high-level language: A high-level language must be compiled or interpreted.
- SQL: SQL is a database query language that must be processed by a DBMS.

questions.stem: A translator that converts a whole high-level program into object code before it is run is
questions.explanation:
A compiler translates the whole source program in one go and produces an object-code file, which can then be run many times without the compiler.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- an interpreter: An interpreter translates and runs one statement at a time.
- an assembler: An assembler translates assembly language, not a high-level language.
- a device driver: A device driver lets the operating system control a hardware device.

questions.stem: Which of the following uses mnemonics such as ADD, SUB and MOV?
questions.explanation:
Assembly language replaces each binary instruction with a short memorable word (a mnemonic). An assembler translates it into machine code.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- machine language: Machine language uses binary codes, not words.
- a high-level language: High-level languages use English-like statements such as PRINT or total = a + b.
- a fourth-generation language: Fourth-generation languages such as SQL use near-English commands for databases.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a high-level programming language?
questions.explanation:
Python, Java, C, BASIC, Pascal, COBOL and FORTRAN are high-level languages: English-like, easier to write and portable between computers.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- machine code: Machine code is the lowest-level language.
- assembly language: Assembly language is a low-level language.
- an assembler: An assembler is a translator, not a language.

questions.stem: An interpreter differs from a compiler because an interpreter
questions.explanation:
An interpreter translates each statement and runs it before going on to the next, so it stops at the first error; it must be present every time the program runs.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- produces an object-code file: A compiler produces object code; an interpreter does not.
- translates the whole program before it is run: That is how a compiler works.
- translates assembly language into machine code: That is the job of an assembler.

options.label: B
options.content: translates the whole program before it is run

options.label: C
options.content: translates and runs a program one statement at a time

options.label: D
options.content: translates assembly language into machine code

questions.stem: COBOL was designed mainly for
questions.explanation:
COBOL stands for COmmon Business-Oriented Language; it is used for business records such as payroll, banking and insurance.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- scientific and engineering calculations: FORTRAN was designed for scientific work.
- teaching beginners to program: BASIC was designed for beginners.
- building websites: JavaScript and PHP are used for websites.

questions.stem: An advantage of high-level languages over low-level languages is that high-level programs
questions.explanation:
High-level languages are machine-independent: the same source program can be translated for different computers. They are also easier to read, write and correct.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- run faster than machine code: Low-level programs usually run faster.
- need no translation: High-level programs must be compiled or interpreted.
- give direct control of the processor's registers: That is a feature of low-level languages.

options.label: A
options.content: can run on different types of computer (are portable)

options.label: D
options.content: give direct control of the processor's registers

papers.title: Basic Computer Operations: practice set 1
papers.description: 7 original WASSCE-style objective questions on basic computer operations, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Restarting a computer that is already switched on is called
questions.explanation:
Warm (soft) booting restarts a running computer, using Restart or Ctrl + Alt + Delete, without switching off the power. It is used after installing software or when a program hangs.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- cold booting: Cold booting starts a computer from the off state.
- logging off: Logging off ends a user's session without restarting the computer.
- hibernating: Hibernating saves the work to disk and switches off.

questions.stem: The checks that the BIOS makes on the hardware when a computer is switched on are called
questions.explanation:
During booting, the BIOS runs the power-on self-test to check the memory, keyboard and disks. If a fault is found it shows a message or gives beeps.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- defragmentation: Defragmentation rearranges files on a hard disk.
- formatting: Formatting prepares a disk for use.
- a virus scan: A virus scan is done by an antivirus program after start-up.

questions.stem: Which keyboard shortcut undoes the last action?
questions.explanation:
Ctrl + Z undoes the last action, Ctrl + Y redoes it, Ctrl + C copies, Ctrl + X cuts and Ctrl + V pastes.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Ctrl + Y: Ctrl + Y redoes an action that was undone.
- Ctrl + U: Ctrl + U underlines selected text.
- Ctrl + X: Ctrl + X cuts selected items.

questions.stem: Right-clicking an item on the desktop usually
questions.explanation:
A right-click shows a shortcut (context) menu of commands for that item, such as Open, Copy, Rename, Delete and Properties.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- opens the item: Double-clicking opens an item.
- deletes the item: Items are deleted with the Delete key or the Delete command.
- moves the item to another folder: Dragging and dropping moves an item.

options.label: A
options.content: shows a shortcut menu of options

options.label: D
options.content: moves the item to another folder

questions.stem: Which device keeps a computer running for a short time when the mains electricity fails?
questions.explanation:
A UPS has a battery that takes over at once when the power fails, giving time to save work and shut down properly.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a stabiliser: A stabiliser keeps the voltage steady but has no battery.
- a surge protector: A surge protector blocks sudden voltage spikes but cannot supply power.
- a modem: A modem connects a computer to the Internet.

questions.stem: Why should a computer be shut down properly rather than switched off at the socket?
questions.explanation:
Shutting down closes programs and saves settings in order. Cutting the power can lose unsaved work and corrupt open files and the operating system.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- to empty the Recycle Bin: Shutting down does not empty the Recycle Bin.
- to make the screen brighter at the next start: Shutting down has nothing to do with screen brightness.
- to delete the user's documents: Shutting down keeps the user's saved documents.

options.label: B
options.content: to make the screen brighter at the next start

options.label: C
options.content: to avoid losing unsaved work and damaging files

questions.stem: Clicking the minimise button of a window
questions.explanation:
A minimised window disappears from view but its program keeps running; clicking its taskbar button brings it back.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- closes the program: The close button (×) closes a program.
- makes the window fill the whole screen: The maximise button does that.
- deletes the open document: Minimising does not change or delete any document.

options.label: B
options.content: makes the window fill the whole screen

options.label: D
options.content: hides the window as a button on the taskbar while the program keeps running

papers.title: File and Folder Management: practice set 1
papers.description: 7 original WASSCE-style objective questions on file and folder management, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: A file named results.xlsx was most likely created with
questions.explanation:
The extension .xlsx shows a Microsoft Excel workbook, a spreadsheet file.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a word processor: Word-processed documents usually end in .docx.
- a presentation program: Presentations usually end in .pptx.
- a database program: Access databases usually end in .accdb.

questions.stem: In the path C:\School\SSS3\ICT\notes.docx, which folder directly contains the file notes.docx?
questions.explanation:
A path lists the drive and then each folder in turn, down to the file. The name just before the file name, ICT, is the folder that holds it.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- SSS3: SSS3 contains the folder ICT, not the file itself.
- School: School is two levels above ICT.
- C:: C: is the root directory of the drive.

questions.stem: Which command saves a copy of a document with a new name, leaving the original unchanged?
questions.explanation:
Save As stores the document under a new name, in a new place or in a new format. The original file stays as it was.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Save: Save stores the changes under the same name and place.
- Rename: Rename changes the name of the existing file; no copy is made.
- Cut: Cut removes a selection so that it can be moved.

questions.stem: Files deleted from the hard disk with the Delete key are first sent to
questions.explanation:
Deleted files go to the Recycle Bin, from which they can be restored until the bin is emptied. Shift + Delete removes a file permanently.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the Clipboard: The Clipboard holds items that have been copied or cut.
- the desktop: The desktop is the main screen; it does not collect deleted files.
- the Documents folder: Documents is where files are usually saved, not deleted to.

questions.stem: Moving a file, rather than copying it,
questions.explanation:
Moving (Cut, then Paste) leaves one file, in its new place. Copying (Copy, then Paste) leaves two: the original and the copy.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- leaves the original and places a copy in the new location: That describes copying.
- makes the file smaller: File compression makes files smaller.
- changes the file's extension: Moving does not change the file's name or type.

options.label: A
options.content: removes it from its old location and places it in the new one

options.label: B
options.content: leaves the original and places a copy in the new location

questions.stem: Which of the following characters is NOT allowed in a Windows file name?
questions.explanation:
Windows file names may not contain a backslash, forward slash, colon, asterisk, question mark, quotation mark, less-than or greater-than sign or vertical bar, because these characters have special meanings to the operating system.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the hyphen (-): A hyphen is allowed, as in term-1.docx.
- the underscore (_): An underscore is allowed, as in my_notes.docx.
- the full stop (.): A full stop is allowed; one separates the name from the extension.

questions.stem: Making files smaller so that they use less storage space and are quicker to send is called
questions.explanation:
Compression programs reduce file size, often producing a .zip file. The files are extracted (decompressed) before use.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- backing up: A backup is a spare copy of files kept for safety.
- formatting: Formatting prepares a disk for use and erases it.
- defragmentation: Defragmentation rearranges files on a hard disk to load faster.

papers.title: Word Processing: practice set 1
papers.description: 7 original WASSCE-style objective questions on word processing, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: The alignment that makes the lines of a paragraph even at both the left and the right margins is
questions.explanation:
Justified text is spaced out so that every full line starts at the left margin and ends at the right margin, as in newspapers and books.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- centre: Centre places each line in the middle of the page.
- left: Left alignment leaves the right edge ragged.
- right: Right alignment leaves the left edge ragged.

questions.stem: Text repeated at the bottom of every page of a document, such as page numbers, is placed in the
questions.explanation:
A footer appears at the bottom of every page and a header at the top; both often hold page numbers, the title or the date.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- header: The header is at the top of every page.
- margin: A margin is the blank space around the edge of the page.
- title bar: The title bar is part of the program window, not the page.

questions.stem: The automatic movement of a word to the next line when the current line is full is called
questions.explanation:
With word wrap, the user keeps typing and the word processor moves words to the next line by itself; Enter is pressed only at the end of a paragraph.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- line spacing: Line spacing is the distance between lines.
- indentation: Indentation moves a paragraph in from the margin.
- a page break: A page break starts a new page.

questions.stem: Which feature produces a personalised copy of one letter for each person on a list of names and addresses?
questions.explanation:
Mail merge combines a main document containing merge fields with a data source (the list), making one copy of the letter for each record.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- find and replace: Find and replace changes words throughout one document.
- spelling and grammar check: This checks for errors in the text.
- print preview: Print preview shows how pages will look before printing.

questions.stem: A page that is wider than it is tall is in
questions.explanation:
Orientation is the direction of the page: portrait (tall, the usual choice) or landscape (wide, useful for wide tables and charts).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- portrait orientation: A portrait page is taller than it is wide.
- justified alignment: Alignment describes how lines sit between the margins.
- double line spacing: Line spacing is the space between lines of text.

questions.stem: Which keyboard shortcut makes selected text bold?
questions.explanation:
Ctrl + B bold, Ctrl + I italic and Ctrl + U underline are the character-formatting shortcuts in most word processors.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Ctrl + I: Ctrl + I makes text italic.
- Ctrl + U: Ctrl + U underlines text.
- Ctrl + P: Ctrl + P opens the Print command.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a word processor?
questions.explanation:
Word processors include Microsoft Word, Google Docs, LibreOffice Writer and WPS Writer.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Microsoft Excel: Excel is a spreadsheet program.
- Microsoft Access: Access is a database management system.
- CorelDRAW: CorelDRAW is a graphics program.

papers.title: Spreadsheets: practice set 1
papers.description: 8 original WASSCE-style objective questions on spreadsheets, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: In a spreadsheet, the box where a row and a column meet is called
questions.explanation:
A cell is named by its column letter and row number, such as C4 for column C, row 4.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a range: A range is a block of several cells.
- a worksheet: A worksheet is a whole grid of rows and columns.
- a field: A field is a column in a database table.

questions.stem: How many cells are in the range B2:D5?
questions.explanation:
B2:D5 covers columns B, C and D (3 columns) and rows 2 to 5 (4 rows), so it has $3 \times 4 = 12$ cells.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 8: This counts only 2 columns; B, C and D are 3 columns.
- 9: This counts only 3 rows; rows 2, 3, 4 and 5 are 4 rows.
- 15: This counts 5 rows; rows 2 to 5 are 4 rows.

questions.stem: Cells A1, A2, A3 and A4 contain 8, 12, 5 and 15. What value does =AVERAGE(A1:A4) give?
questions.explanation:
AVERAGE adds the values and divides by how many there are: $(8 + 12 + 5 + 15) \div 4 = 40 \div 4 = 10$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 40: 40 is the sum, given by =SUM(A1:A4).
- 15: 15 is the largest value, given by =MAX(A1:A4).
- 5: 5 is the smallest value, given by =MIN(A1:A4).

questions.stem: The formula =C3+D3 in cell E3 is copied down to cell E6. What does it become?
questions.explanation:
The references are relative. Moving the formula 3 rows down (from row 3 to row 6) adds 3 to each row number: =C3+D3 becomes =C6+D6.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- =C3+D3: The references would stay the same only if they were absolute.
- =F3+G3: Copying down changes the row numbers, not the column letters.
- =C6+D3: Both references are relative, so both row numbers change.

questions.stem: Which type of cell reference does NOT change when a formula is copied to another cell?
questions.explanation:
An absolute reference has a dollar sign before both the column letter and the row number, so it always points to the same cell, such as a fixed exchange rate.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a relative reference: A relative reference changes to keep the same position relative to the new cell.
- a mixed reference: A mixed reference fixes only the column or only the row; the other part changes.
- a range: A range is a block of cells, not a kind of reference.

questions.stem: Every formula in a spreadsheet must begin with
questions.explanation:
The equals sign tells the spreadsheet that the entry is a formula to be calculated. Without it, B2+C2 is treated as a text label.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a cell reference: A formula may contain cell references, but = must come first.
- a bracket: Brackets group parts of a formula; they do not start it.
- the word SUM: SUM is only one of many functions.

questions.stem: Which chart is best for showing how a whole budget is shared between different items?
questions.explanation:
A pie chart shows each item as a slice of a circle, so the parts of a whole, such as a budget, and their shares are easy to see.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a line graph: A line graph shows change over time.
- a scatter chart: A scatter chart shows the relationship between two sets of numbers.
- a column chart: A column chart compares amounts, but does not show them as parts of one whole.

questions.stem: A cell shows ##### instead of a number. This means that
questions.explanation:
##### is not a real error: the number is there but cannot fit. Widening the column shows it.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a formula divides by zero: Dividing by zero shows #DIV/0!.
- a function name is misspelt: A misspelt function shows #NAME?.
- a cell used in the formula has been deleted: A deleted reference shows #REF!.

options.label: C
options.content: a cell used in the formula has been deleted

options.label: D
options.content: the column is too narrow to display the number

papers.title: Databases: practice set 1
papers.description: 7 original WASSCE-style objective questions on databases, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: A field whose value is different for every record, so that it identifies each record, is called
questions.explanation:
The primary key, such as a student ID or account number, is unique to each record, so no two records can be confused.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a foreign key: A foreign key links one table to another table's primary key.
- a query: A query is a request to find records.
- a field name: A field name is just the heading of a column.

questions.stem: In a database table, a row holding all the data about one person is called
questions.explanation:
A table is made of records (rows), one for each person or thing, and fields (columns), one for each item of data.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a field: A field is a column: one item of data about every person.
- a file: A file is a collection of related records.
- a report: A report is a formatted printout of data.

questions.stem: Which database object is used to find the records that meet given conditions?
questions.explanation:
A query asks a question of the database using criteria, such as Class = "SSS3", and shows only the matching records.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a form: A form is used to enter and view records.
- a report: A report presents data neatly for printing.
- a macro: A macro automates a series of actions.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a database management system?
questions.explanation:
Database management systems include Microsoft Access, MySQL, Oracle, Microsoft SQL Server and PostgreSQL.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Microsoft PowerPoint: PowerPoint is presentation software.
- Adobe Photoshop: Photoshop is graphics software.
- Google Chrome: Chrome is a web browser.

questions.stem: Which field would be the most suitable primary key in a table of students?
questions.explanation:
A primary key must never repeat. Each student has a different index number, so it identifies each record uniquely.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- surname: Many students can share a surname.
- class: Many students are in the same class.
- date of birth: Two students can be born on the same day.

questions.stem: A database that stores data in several tables linked by key fields is
questions.explanation:
In a relational database, tables are linked by matching fields, such as StudentID in a Students table and a Fees table. Most databases today are relational.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a flat-file database: A flat-file database has only one table.
- a hierarchical database: A hierarchical database arranges records in a tree.
- a network database: A network database links records in a web of parents, not tables joined by keys.

questions.stem: The most suitable data type for a field that stores phone numbers such as 076123456 is
questions.explanation:
Phone numbers are stored as text because they are not used in calculations and may begin with 0 or a + sign.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- number: A number field would drop the leading 0, and phone numbers are never calculated.
- currency: Currency is for amounts of money.
- yes/no: Yes/No holds only two values.

papers.title: Presentations and Graphics: practice set 1
papers.description: 7 original WASSCE-style objective questions on presentations and graphics, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: In presentation software, the visual effect seen as one slide changes to the next is called
questions.explanation:
Transitions, such as fade, push or wipe, happen between slides; animations happen to objects on a slide.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- an animation: An animation moves an object on a slide.
- a theme: A theme is a set of colours, fonts and backgrounds.
- a layout: A layout is the arrangement of placeholders on a slide.

questions.stem: Which view is best for rearranging the order of the slides in a presentation?
questions.explanation:
Slide Sorter view shows small copies of all the slides together, so they can be dragged into a new order, copied or deleted.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Notes Page view: Notes Page view shows one slide with its speaker notes.
- Slide Show view: Slide Show view displays the slides full-screen to an audience.
- Reading view: Reading view plays the presentation in the window.

questions.stem: In Microsoft PowerPoint, which key starts the slide show from the first slide?
questions.explanation:
F5 starts the show from the first slide and Shift + F5 from the current slide; Esc ends it.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- F1: F1 opens Help.
- F7: F7 starts the spelling check.
- Esc: Esc ends a slide show.

questions.stem: An image made of a grid of pixels, which becomes jagged when it is enlarged, is called
questions.explanation:
Bitmap images, such as photographs, store the colour of every pixel; enlarging them makes the pixels visible, so edges look jagged.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a vector image: A vector image is made of shapes and stays sharp when enlarged.
- a 3D model: A 3D model describes a solid shape in three dimensions.
- a chart: A chart is a picture of numerical data.

questions.stem: Which program is mainly used to create vector graphics such as logos?
questions.explanation:
Drawing (vector) programs include CorelDRAW, Adobe Illustrator and Inkscape. Vector logos print sharply at any size.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Microsoft Paint: Paint edits bitmap (pixel) images.
- Microsoft Excel: Excel is a spreadsheet program.
- Microsoft Access: Access is a database management system.

questions.stem: The slide that stores the design and layout used by every slide in a presentation is called
questions.explanation:
A change made to the slide master, such as a new font or a logo, appears on every slide that uses it.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the title slide: The title slide is the first slide of a presentation.
- the notes pane: The notes pane holds the speaker's notes.
- a placeholder: A placeholder is a box for content on one slide.

questions.stem: Notes that help the presenter but are not shown to the audience are called
questions.explanation:
Speaker notes are typed in the notes pane; the presenter can see or print them, but the audience sees only the slides.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- handouts: Handouts are printed copies of the slides given to the audience.
- placeholders: Placeholders are boxes for content on a slide.
- transitions: Transitions are effects between slides.
